record.field: Start of shift: what came in, what is waiting, how conversion is going.
Six clickable KPI cards plus a contact-status donut, a source-channel bar chart and three live feeds, all filtered by one period selector.
It is the only screen that tells you whether the desk is keeping up. Pending Follow-ups above your team's capacity is the earliest visible sign that somebody will be forgotten.
At the start of every shift, and again before you leave. Not while you are working a single person — use Care Command or Contacts for that.
You need the Owner or CRM role; this leaf is role-gated in the database.
Reading a percentage without the period. Conversion Rate is a month figure; Contacts Today is a day figure. They never describe the same window.
Treating a low Spam Rate as good news. A low rate can also mean nobody is marking spam, which quietly inflates every other number.
Not clicking through. Every card and every chart segment opens the exact records behind it — a surprising number should always be opened, never explained away.
The triage wall: every open conversation across every channel, most urgent first.
One work item per person, merged from Zalo, calls, email and web chat, ordered by a computed urgency score.
Without it, four inboxes each look quiet while the same family is waiting in all four. The wall is the only place the whole picture exists.
All shift. It is where a CRM operator lives; the other screens are what you open from it.
Owner or CRM role, plus at least one connected channel. Taking a conversation off a colleague additionally needs CRM Manager.
Replying without claiming. Two operators answering the same family within a minute of each other is the most common complaint this screen exists to prevent.
Reading the urgency score as a clinical severity. It is a triage number built from status and waiting time. A 110 is not a medical emergency; it is a strong queue position.
Assuming the Zalo account belongs to the patient. In home care it is very often a son or a daughter — and what you may tell them is a consent question, not a convenience question.
The record behind the conversation: status tabs, quick actions, and the booking wizard.
Every enquiry as a record, filtered by lifecycle status, with Book · Log Activity · Log as Lead · Escalate · Spam · Booking Lost on each row and on the form.
Care Command is the queue; this is the ledger. A conversation can be closed, but the contact's status is what the Dashboard counts and what the next operator inherits.
When you need the whole person rather than the current message — booking them in, recording why a booking was lost, or checking what a colleague did last week.
Owner or CRM role. Booking additionally needs a service, a facility and a date/time.
Skipping the duplicate check in the booking wizard. Confirming the wrong suggested client writes the visit — and later the clinical note — into another person's record.
Using Spam as a way to clear the list. Spam also flags the phone number, so a real family member is pre-judged the next time they call.
Leaving a lost booking un-reasoned. “Booking Lost” without a reason is invisible to Lead Analysis, so the same cause repeats all quarter.
The team's shared follow-up board — every scheduled call, meeting, email and task.
Everything anyone scheduled on a contact, grouped by type (To-Do · Email · Call · Meeting · Document) with a type filter and a date filter.
A promise made on Monday is only kept if it is visible on Thursday. This board is the difference between “we'll call you back” and being called back.
Twice a day: at the start of the shift, and before handover at {{handoverTime}}. Also whenever the Dashboard's Pending Follow-ups number surprises you.
Owner or CRM role. An activity must be scheduled on a contact — it cannot exist on its own.
Scheduling on yourself out of habit. An activity assigned to one person is invisible as team work; if you are off sick it simply does not happen.
Closing an activity without recording the outcome on the contact. The board goes green, the contact's status stays wrong, and the Dashboard lies.
Filtering to Today and forgetting overdue items are not in that filter.
Things that arrived on a channel but carried too little to become a conversation.
An immutable record of exactly what arrived — a Facebook comment with no phone, a webhook with no identity. You convert it or dismiss it; you cannot edit it.
A queue nobody can find is a queue that does not exist. These are real people who reached out and would otherwise vanish between systems.
Once or twice a shift, and always after a campaign goes live — that is when the volume of half-identified arrivals jumps.
Visible to every role. Converting needs at least one anchor: a contact, a phone number or an email address.
Dismissing to clear the badge. Dismissal is an answer — “this was not a patient” — and it is recorded against your name.
Trying to correct what arrived. The record is deliberately un-editable: it is evidence of what the channel actually sent.
Converting a capture with no anchor and being surprised it refuses — there would be no way to reach the person again.
Connect, prove and watch every channel. The most consequential setup screen in CRM.
A catalogue of the eight connectable channels with a lifecycle state each, the readiness checks behind that state, and the go-live console.
Configured is not connected. A channel that leaves the connected states stops sending and can stop receiving — and nothing queues. Patients get silence, and the wall looks calm.
At go-live, when a grant is expiring, and the moment a channel's traffic drops to zero. Not during a shift by a shift operator.
Visible to every role, but the state has exactly one writer — a server transition path. You cannot type a state in.
Choosing the wrong Official Account at the “choose what to connect” step. One OA serves one catchment area, so the wrong one routes a whole city's messages into another city's wall.
Ignoring “Expiring soon”. It still sends today, which is exactly why it gets ignored until the day it does not.
Reading a green tick as proof of delivery. The readiness checks prove the connection is capable; only real traffic proves it works.
Every arrival from the website, with the advert or link that produced it.
One row per website arrival: page, referrer, UTM source/medium/campaign, and the Google or Facebook click id — plus an “Unmatched campaigns” chip for arrivals with no tags.
It is the only honest answer to “which advert is actually producing bookings”. Without it, budget follows opinion.
Weekly, and whenever a campaign's cost per enquiry looks wrong. Also when a specific person asks “how did you get my number”.
Visible to every role. A touchpoint is created by the website connector; you never type one in.
Assuming the touchpoint and the conversation share a channel. Someone can click a Google advert on Monday and message Zalo on Wednesday; they are joined by phone number, not by channel.
Treating “Unmatched campaigns” as noise. It is usually a link somebody published without tags — a fixable, repeating leak.
Counting touchpoints as people. One person browsing four pages is four touchpoints and one enquiry.
The pivot: enquiries by source, status, service and area — the whole funnel in one grid.
The same contact records as Contacts, in list, pivot and graph modes, so you can cross any two dimensions.
The Dashboard tells you the number. This tells you which combination produced it — which channel, in which area, for which service.
Monthly review, campaign post-mortems, and any argument about where enquiries come from.
Visible to every role. Numbers only reconcile with the Dashboard if you match the period and the catchment filter.
Comparing this month's pivot with the Dashboard's Today card and calling it a discrepancy.
Grouping by declared channel when the traffic says otherwise. Effective channel is the field that reflects what actually happened.
Reading a small cell as a trend. Six referrals in a month is a number, not a pattern.
The day in six numbers, and the one that matters is Unassigned.
Six counts for one day in one catchment area — booked, unassigned, in progress, completed, staff on shift, cancelled — with the unassigned bookings listed underneath.
Five of the six are reassurance. Unassigned is the one that turns into a patient ringing to ask where the nurse is, and it is the only number here you can still fix today.
First thing in the morning, again after lunch, and before you leave. It is a whole-day view, so checking it hourly tells you nothing new.
Operations Manager or Owner. A nurse does not see this screen — they see their own visits, not the day.
Reading Completed as progress. Two completed at 11:00 is normal; two completed at 16:00 means the afternoon has not started.
Treating Cancelled as neutral. A cancellation still consumed a slot someone else could have had, and it has a reason worth reading.
Checking the number and not the list. The count tells you there is a problem; the list underneath tells you whose problem it is.
Every visit for the day, and the four things you can do to one.
One row per visit with its time, patient, service, district, assigned person and state — draft, new, assigned, in progress, completed, cancelled, closed.
It is the only screen where a visit exists as a whole thing rather than as a row on somebody's schedule. Assigning, moving and cancelling all happen here.
Whenever something changes: a nurse calls in sick, a patient rings to move a time, a booking arrives with nobody on it.
Operations Manager or Owner. Cancelling additionally destroys revenue, so it is worth knowing before you press it that nothing here asks twice.
Cancelling when you meant to reschedule. Cancel ends the visit and the money; reschedule keeps both and moves them.
Assigning without looking at the map. A visit that fits the calendar can still be impossible to reach in time.
Leaving a booking unassigned because it is not urgent yet. Unassigned at 09:00 is a scheduling task; unassigned at 15:00 is a phone call to a family.
Who is doing what, all day — the screen an Operations Manager lives in.
One row per person for one day, their visits along it, their load against capacity, and the leave that touches this week.
Bookings tells you what was promised. This tells you whether it can actually be done by the people who are actually here.
Before the shift, and every time somebody becomes unavailable. It is also where you find out what approving a leave request just cost.
Operations Manager or Owner. Reassigning someone else's visit is the whole point of the screen, so it is not available to the nurse whose visit it is.
Reading an empty row as a free nurse. An unassigned booking is not on anyone's row — the gap you are looking at may already be spoken for.
Balancing by count alone. Five short visits in one district is a lighter day than three spread across the city.
Approving leave from the leave screen without coming here. Approval does not move the visits already booked for that day.
Load against capacity, per person — the fairness check.
A bar per person: visits assigned today against their capacity for the day.
The schedule shows you the shape of the day. This shows you whether it is fair, and an unfair day is the one that produces sick leave next week.
After you finish assigning, not before. It is a check on decisions already made.
Reading capacity as hours. It is visits per day, and two visits in one building are not two visits across two districts.
Aiming for everyone at the same number. Equal counts across unequal distances is not fairness.
Leave requests — and the visits they quietly collide with.
Requests with who, which dates, what kind, and whether they are approved.
Approving leave is the single most common way a fully-booked day becomes an unstaffed one, because approval and the schedule are two different screens.
As requests arrive — and always with the Staff Schedule open beside it for the dates concerned.
Operations Manager or Owner. A nurse can request; only Operations can approve.
Approving without opening the schedule for those dates. Approval does not move a single visit — it just makes the person unavailable for visits that are still booked.
Leaving a request sitting. An unanswered request is a person who has already made plans.
Cash the nurses are holding right now, and who reconciles it.
How much cash each member of staff is carrying from today's visits, and the total.
This is money that exists physically and has to end up matching. It is reconciled inside Operations at end of shift; Finance receives one balanced figure and never chases an individual nurse.
End of every shift, without exception. A day skipped is a day nobody can reconstruct.
Operations Manager or Owner. Finance sees the result, not this screen.
Sending an unbalanced figure to Finance to sort out. It is settled here first — that is the whole reason this screen sits in Operations.
Reconciling from memory at the end of a long shift. The visit list is right there and it does not get tired.
The patient record a visit is booked against.
Clients in your catchment area, with the record behind each: their consents, their history and their balance.
A booking points at a client. If the client is wrong or duplicated, the visit, the clinical note and the invoice all end up in the wrong place together.
Before booking someone you are not certain about, and whenever a name looks familiar.
Operations Manager, Owner — and CRM, which is the one OPS screen the reception desk can also open.
Creating a second record because the first was hard to find. Their consents and balance stay on the first one.
Messages from relatives about a patient — and what you may answer.
Two-way messages between a family member and the care team, attached to the client rather than to a phone number.
Most 'where is the nurse' calls arrive here first. Answering the logistics question fast is usually all that is needed — and it is the part you are always allowed to answer.
Through the shift, and especially in the hour before a visit when families start to wonder.
Operations Manager or Owner. What you may say about the patient's condition is a recorded consent, not a judgement call.
Answering a clinical question because it was asked kindly. Timing is yours to answer; condition is not.
Assuming the sender is allowed to hear everything because they are family. Relationship is not consent.
Whether a person can actually get from one visit to the next.
The travel time between two consecutive visits, against the gap between them — with a verdict.
The calendar cannot see the map. A visit at 15:00 in one district and 16:30 in another fits perfectly on a schedule and may be impossible in traffic.
Whenever you reassign across districts, and before you promise a family a time.
Treating the warning as a block. It warns and lets you save, because a manager on the phone often knows something the map does not.
Treating the absence of a warning as a promise. It knows distance, not weather, lifts, or how long a family keeps you at the door.
The month in money: billed, paid, outstanding, and what is overdue.
Billed, collected and outstanding for one month in one catchment area, with the overdue figure broken out.
Outstanding is not a problem; overdue is. The gap between them is the whole job of this section — 6,150,000 ₫ owed of which 1,850,000 ₫ has passed its terms.
Start of the day and at month end. It is a month view, so a figure that moves hourly is a figure you are misreading.
Accountant or Owner. An Operations Manager sees Invoices but not this screen.
Reading Outstanding as debt. Most of it is simply invoices younger than their payment terms.
Comparing this month with last without the same catchment area. The area selector changes every figure on the screen.
Sixty-three invoices, and the one action on them that cannot be undone.
Every customer invoice for the month with its state — draft, posted, paid — the client, the service and the amount.

Posting an invoice locks it into a legal sequence. A draft is a document you are still writing; a posted invoice is a document that exists, and the only way back is a credit note, which is itself a document.
Whenever a visit completes and needs billing, and whenever a posted invoice turns out to be wrong.
Accountant, Owner — and the Operations Manager, who can see invoices because a booking question is often an invoice question.
Posting to tidy the list. Draft is a valid resting state; posted is a commitment with a number attached.
Editing after posting. The fields that matter are locked, and the ones that are not do not change the document that was issued.
What has actually arrived, against what was invoiced.
Every payment received this month and which invoice it settled — 48 of the 63 invoices are paid.
An invoice is a claim; a payment is a fact. This is the screen that turns one into the other, and the difference between them is what the AR screens chase.
Daily. A payment recorded late is an invoice that was chased for no reason.
Recording a payment against the client rather than the invoice. The client's balance looks right and the invoice stays open.
A read-only record of what was posted.
Posted customer invoices, listed. It is a record, not a working document — there is no form behind it to open and edit.
When somebody asks what was issued in a period, this is the answer, and its read-only nature is the point: the log and the filing cannot disagree.
At period end, and whenever a figure needs to be traced back to the documents behind it.
Expecting to correct something here. Nothing on this screen changes a document — corrections happen on the invoice, and after posting that means a credit note.
Receivables by age — the shape of what is owed.
Outstanding money grouped by how long it has been outstanding, so a total becomes a set of different problems.

6,150,000 ₫ owed sounds like one problem. Split by age it is fifteen invoices, four of which have passed their terms and one of which is 47 days old — and only that last group needs a phone call today.
Weekly, and before any conversation about cash flow.
Chasing the largest balance first. The oldest is nearly always the one at risk, not the biggest.
The working screen for receivables, with three tools under it.
The place receivables are actually worked, with Account Payment, Cash In Transit and Refund / Credit grouped beneath it.
The dashboard tells you the shape; this is where something happens about it.
Whenever the AR Dashboard shows something that needs a decision rather than a look.
Treating its three children as separate screens. They are three answers to one question — money that has not settled.
The four invoices that have passed their terms.
Clients with invoices past their payment terms, oldest first — four this month, 1,850,000 ₫ between them.
This is the only receivables screen that is a to-do list. Everything else describes; this one asks you to ring somebody.
Weekly, and always before month end.
Chasing before checking Payments. A payment recorded late looks exactly like a payment never made, and the client remembers being chased for it.
Every movement on a receivable, in order.
The audit trail behind a balance: what was invoiced, what was paid, what was credited and when.
When a client disputes a balance, this is the screen that answers it. A balance is an opinion until you can show the movements.
When a figure is questioned, and before writing anything off.
Reading the balance without the movements. The balance is the result; the movements are the reason, and only one of those settles an argument.
Recording money against the right invoice.
Where a received payment is matched to what it settles.
A payment against the client instead of the invoice leaves the balance right and the invoice open — so the client is chased for money they have already paid.
Part-paying without saying which invoice. The system cannot guess, and the oldest is not always what the client intended.
Cash collected on a visit that has not reached the bank yet.
Money that exists physically and is between a nurse's pocket and the account — 1,350,000 ₫ tonight.
Operations reconciles this at end of shift and hands Finance one balanced figure. Finance never chases an individual nurse — if it does not balance, Operations settles it first.
Daily, as the balanced figure arrives from Operations.
Accountant or Owner. The collecting happens in Operations, on their own screen.
Going to the nurse when it does not balance. That is Operations' job and their screen — going round them is how one person ends up asked twice.
Vietnamese tax invoices — the most consequential screen in the product.
Every red invoice issued through Viettel, its state, and whether it has been cancelled — 41 issued this month, 1 cancelled.
A red invoice is a tax document, not a record in this system. Issuing it files it; cancelling it is a filing event too, and the buyer may already be holding a copy.
When a client asks for one, and when an issued one turns out to be wrong.
Cancelling requires the Vietnamese Tax Compliance permission — deliberately narrower than Accountant, because it is the one action here that reaches outside the clinic.
Cancelling to correct a small mistake after the filing period has closed. Inside the period, cancel and reissue; after it, the route is a credit note.
Treating it like an internal document. The buyer holds a copy, and the tax authority holds a record — neither of them sees your correction unless it is filed.
Three different situations that all look like giving money back.
Prepaid credit returned, an unfinished package refunded pro-rata, and a mistaken payment reversed. Three routes, three different records.

The route decides what happens to the client's history. A transaction reversal is a correction — it says the payment should never have been recorded. A package refund says the course stopped early. Choosing the wrong one leaves the client's record telling a story that did not happen.
Whenever money goes back — and before deciding the amount, because the route decides the amount.
Picking the route by whichever screen you happen to be standing on. That is the most common way the wrong one gets used.
Refunding a whole package when four of eight visits were delivered. Pro-rata is not a courtesy — it is what the client actually consumed.
Courses of visits sold up front.
Packages available and sold — a wound-care course of 8 and a physiotherapy course of 8 this month.
A package is money taken before the service is delivered, so it is a liability until the visits happen. That is why an unfinished one is refunded pro-rata rather than argued about.
When selling one, and whenever a course stops early.
Treating a sold package as revenue. It becomes revenue one visit at a time.
Social health insurance claims — not in use yet.
The screen where claims against a patient's BHYT entitlement will be prepared and tracked. Nothing is being submitted through it today.
Written honestly as not-yet-in-use rather than teaching a workflow nobody runs. When it is switched on this outline becomes a lesson; until then, knowing it exists and is not live is the useful fact.
Not yet. If a claim needs making today it is happening outside this system.
Assuming a visit is covered because the screen exists. Nothing here has been submitted, so nothing here has been accepted.
